prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

WASHINGTON (CNN)  -- First lady Michelle Obama's father is not buried in the Chicago-area cemetery where investigators say hundreds of graves have been dug up in a scheme to resell the burial plots, a spokeswoman said Tuesday. First lady Michelle Obama's father is not buried in the Chicago-area cemetery where graves were disturbed. The announcement followed an earlier, mistaken statement by the first lady's communications director, Camille Johnston. Johnston later said that Obama's father, Fraser Robinson III, was buried in Lincoln Cemetery in suburban Alsip, Illinois, not the Burr Oak graveyard now at the center of a criminal investigation. "There has been some confusion that has been cleared up," Johnston said. Robinson, who worked as a pump operator for the Chicago water department, died in 1991 after a long struggle with multiple sclerosis. Lincoln Cemetery is about 2 miles from Burr Oak. Four people face felony charges in the investigation surrounding Burr Oak Cemetery in Alsip, Illinois. Authorities said last week that about 300 graves had been disturbed as part of the scheme, but that number is expected to rise. Cook County Sheriff Thomas Dart said his office has received more than 55,000 requests for information from families with loved ones buried in Burr Oak. But he said many of the cemetery's records are in rusted cabinets filled with decaying file cards. "Most of the file cards have rotted together," he said. "They're covered in mold, and they've rotted together." In addition, some of the cemetery's books are missing pages, and others are known to have been altered, "So this has made it incredibly difficult for us to give accurate information," Dart said. His office asked a court Tuesday to appoint a receiver to manage the graveyard, which he said has been run by his office since last week. Among others buried in the 150-acre graveyard are civil rights martyr Emmett Till, blues pioneer Willie Dixon, jazz and blues singer Dinah Washington and several Negro League baseball players. Cemetery groundskeepers told investigators that Till's grave was not among those disturbed, but the identities of other remains dug up have not been disclosed. Carolyn Towns, an office manager for the cemetery, and gravediggers Keith Nicks, Terrance Nicks and Maurice Daley have each been charged with dismembering a human body. The felony charge carries a sentence ranging from six to 30 years, authorities said. Authorities began investigating the cemetery about six weeks ago after receiving a call from its owners, who said they suspected "financial irregularities" regarding the business, Cook County Sheriff Thomas Dart told CNN last week. He said the owners are not believed to be involved in the alleged scam. CNN correspondents Dan Lothian and Elaine Quijano contributed to this report.

**Alsip, Illinois** — Authorities have charged four cemetery workers in connection with a scheme to dig up graves, dispose of human remains, and resell burial plots at the historic Burr Oak Cemetery, a predominantly African American cemetery known as the resting place of civil rights-era figures.

## The Charges

Cook County Sheriff Thomas Dart announced that four employees were arrested and charged with felony counts of dismembering a human body. Those charged included Carolyn Towns, a cemetery manager, along with three gravediggers: Keith Nicks, Terrence Nicks, and Maurice Dailey.

According to investigators, the workers allegedly dug up hundreds of graves, discarded the remains—sometimes in a remote, overgrown area of the cemetery—and resold the emptied plots to unsuspecting families. Authorities estimated the scheme may have generated hundreds of thousands of dollars.

Sheriff Dart described the operation in stark terms, detailing how bones and remains were dumped and how caskets were crushed and discarded to make room to resell space.

## Historic Significance

Burr Oak Cemetery holds particular importance in African American history. Among those buried there is Emmett Till, the 14-year-old whose 1955 lynching helped galvanize the civil rights movement. Investigators reported finding Till's original glass-topped casket—which had been part of his famous open-casket funeral—neglected in a rundown storage area, deepening public outrage over the case.

The cemetery is also the burial site of noted blues musicians and other prominent figures, drawing added national attention to the desecration.

## Investigative Challenges

Investigators faced significant obstacles in determining the full scope of the scheme and identifying affected families. Officials reported that cemetery records were disorganized, incomplete, or in some cases deliberately altered and damaged, making it extremely difficult to establish which graves had been disturbed and where remains belonged.

The poor state of recordkeeping complicated efforts to match plots to the families who had purchased them, and to account for remains that had been removed. Authorities anticipated that fully reconstructing burial records and confirming the identities and locations of the deceased would be a lengthy and painstaking process.

The Cook County Sheriff's Office established a hotline to field inquiries from concerned families, receiving thousands of calls from people worried about the fate of loved ones interred at the cemetery.

## Aftermath

The revelations prompted grief and anger among families with relatives buried at Burr Oak, many of whom traveled to the site seeking assurance that their loved ones' graves had not been disturbed. The case raised broader questions about oversight of cemeteries and the safeguarding of burial records, leading to calls for stronger regulation of the funeral and cemetery industry.

*This report reflects information released by the Cook County Sheriff's Office and authorities during the investigation.*
